newsitem.title: CHINA: FEATURE - China insurer girds for competition.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - China insurer girds for competition.

text.p: China's biggest insurance group -- People's Insurance -- once had the domestic market all to itself but now it must hustle for its share of the business.
New competitors and an insurance law passed last year have meant big changes in the way People's Insurance -- now known as the People's Insurance Company of China (Group) -- does business.
"We had been a monopoly operating under central planning," Song Shuguang, head of the group's policy research section, said in a recent interview.
"We had administrative regulations requiring the purchase of insurance. But now we are a commercial entity."
The big insurer still dominates the domestic market, taking some 79 percent of all premiums.

The market, where many people have still never heard of insurance, is growing rapidly, and premiums are seen rising to 200 to 250 billion yuan ($24-30 billion) by 2000 from 61.6 billion yuan last year. But the field is becoming a bit more crowded.

Five new domestic companies have gained approval to begin operations this year, swelling the ranks of insurers that already include successful entrants such as Ping An Insurance and Taiping Insurance, both state-owned like People's Insurance.
China has been very slow in letting foreign competitors into the market but a few firms are making their presence felt.
Manufacturers Life Insurance Co of Canada is forming a joint venture with a cash-rich domestic partner, oil trader Sinochem.
Japan's Tokio Marine and Fire Insurance and American International Assurance Co Ltd (AIA) have been allowed into the Shanghai market, where AIA has been particularly aggressive.
"The new companies will have an impact on our business," Song said. "We used to be the only game in town."
Competitors are poaching their experienced employees and giving sales staff hefty commissions, forcing a rethink of strategy at People's Insurance.
"We are moving in the same direction on commissions," said Song.
At the same time, the group has had to restructure to conform with the new regulatory environment, overseen by the People's Bank of China, the central bank.
People's Insurance has set up separate property and life insurance companies as well as a reinsurance unit. All three arms of the company have been reorganised under a holding company.
"This brings us in line with practices overseas -- you don't want a single company using its steady stream of life insurance premiums to fund its property insurance operations," Song said.

Property, however, is the group's big money spinner. The group's total premiums in the first half of the year were 29 billion yuan -- with 19.9 billion from property insurance and about 9 billion from life insurance.
Song did not disclose first-half profits but in all of 1995 the group earned 1.6 billion yuan on premium income of 47.6 billion.
Profits this year would depend on the final tally of damage from widespread flooding in central, southern and northern China this summer, said the official.
People's Insurance has said payments on flood claims could reach 3.2 billion yuan. In the northern province of Hebei alone it compensated more than 2,400 enterprises and 15,000 families.
People's Insurance is now a limited company, and in future it hopes to become a shareholding company -- the first step in a drive to offer shares on the domestic or foreign markets.
"Issuing stock is a medium-term goal -- perhaps four or five years from now," said Song.

The group also has new restrictions on what it can do with its income. China's insurance law restricts investments to government bonds, bank deposits and certain projects approved by the State Council, or cabinet.
The new developments in the market have also led the group to believe that as competition intensifies, a link with foreign insurance companies might prove useful.
"We are looking for a big partner," said the official, adding that any cooperation would be in a specialised segment of the market.
"Competition is forcing us to improve."
